preferenceInterpretation.systemPrompt:
Interpret the user's supplemental tourism preferences into normalized intent.
Return JSON only. You interpret language; deterministic code enforces the result.
Never invent geographic entities, provider IDs, coordinates, or evidence.
Do not turn ambiguity into a hard rule. Preserve uncertainty in ambiguities.
For positive preferences, output preferredFacets as a list of objects with:
- dimension: active dimension name (theme, trait, intent, winery_scale, tourism_intensity, nature_type, local_character). Do NOT output exploration_style.
- key: CANONICAL domain key in English (e.g. "architecture" not "arquitectura", "food" not "comida", "walk" not "caminata", "history" not "historia").
- Map history to theme and walk to intent. nature_type is only for mountain, forest, coast, river, desert, or park. local_character is only for authentic, residential, traditional, or contemporary. A named neighborhood such as San Telmo is an anchor, not local_character.
- confidence: float between 0 and 1 indicating certainty.
- strength: "strong" | "medium" | "weak" indicating user emphasis.
- evidence: one or more short excerpts copied from the user's text that support
  this facet. Never invent evidence; facets without supporting excerpts are rejected.
Do not invent arbitrary importance numbers; code derives importance deterministically from strength.
Also output anchoredPlaces: concrete named places/areas/routes the user explicitly mentioned by
name (never a generic theme). For each, output:
- rawName: the name as mentioned by the user.
- usage: "geographic_scope" | "specific_destination" | "named_path" | "unknown". This describes how the phrase uses the name, not what geographic entity it is.
- priority: "must" ONLY for explicit, unambiguous named-place intent, for example
  "quiero visitar X", "incluí X", "sí o sí quiero ir a X", "no me quiero perder X".
  Anything weaker or ambiguous -- including a place mentioned only in passing while
  describing a theme, e.g. "me interesa la arquitectura de X" -- is priority "soft".
Extract anchors conservatively: when in doubt about the name or the intent, omit the anchor
rather than guessing. Do not invent named places that were not mentioned.
Other fields: excludedThemes, excludedTraits, hardExclusions, softConstraints, ambiguities,
dietaryPreferences, accessibilityPreferences, budgetPreferences, groupPreferences,
positiveSemanticQuery, notes. Use short lowercase phrases.

San Telmo is the oldest, most atmospheric neighborhood in Buenos Aires, brimming with 19th-century architecture, cobblestone streets, and deep tango roots.
A historical walking tour of San Telmo typically covers these iconic highlights and key stops:
DirectionsWebsiteThe historic heart of the neighborhood, famous for its Sunday antique market, street tango dancers, and surrounding cafes.
CallDirectionsWebsiteA bustling 19th-century market filled with vintage stalls, local produce, and amazing food vendors.
CallDirectionsWebsiteThe narrowest house in Buenos Aires (just 2.2 meters wide), wrapped in local folklore about freed slaves and colonial history.
CallDirectionsThe popular photo-op corner (Chile and Defensa) featuring Argentina's beloved comic strip character created by Quino.
CallDirectionsWebsiteFascinating underground brick tunnels and restored colonial patios that reveal the hidden streams and early history of the city.
DirectionsWebsiteA lush, historic green space widely considered the traditional site of Pedro de Mendoza's first (and failed) founding of Buenos Aires in 1536.

evidence.title: Manzana de las Luces
evidence.snippet: Este bloque, rodeado de las calles Alsina, Moreno, Perú y Bolívar, es el hogar de muchos de los más importantes y tradicionales de educación, instituciones religiosas y culturales de Buenos Aires, que datan del siglo 17 y 18. El nombre de este bloque proviene del número de instituciones intelectuales que estaban presentes en los viejos tiempos. Una de las atracciones más interesantes es una red subterránea de túneles misteriosos que comunica cada edificio.

evidence.title: Mercado San Telmo
evidence.snippet: mercado alojado en una sala enorme Wrough-hierro. Todo, desde la albahaca fresca para zapatos y monedas antiguas se encuentra en exhibición en este mercado permanente. Venir durante la semana para ver el mercado de productos y la carne local. El domingo, cuando la acción está fuera, es prácticamente vacío.

evidence.title: Plaza Dorrego
evidence.snippet: La segunda plaza más antigua de Buenos Aires, seis días a la semana, la plaza es un espacio relativamente tranquilo, con sombra junto a restaurantes y cafés. Los domingos un mercado de antigüedades se hace cargo y casi no se puede ver la plaza del pueblo y puestos de mercado. Los puestos de ser anulado distancia de aproximadamente 17:00, y de 20:00 Hay baile público, incluyendo el tango.
